social.title: Mithila Painting Before and Beyond the Modern Art Market
social.part: Part Vi — Material Culture And The Arts
social.summary: Mithila painting presents a paradox for the social historian. The practice is repeatedly described as old, yet its most durable and datable corpus is overwhelmingly modern because the older media were intentionally temporary. Floor diagrams were renewed, mud-plastered walls were resurfaced, pigments faded, houses were rebuilt, and floods, earthquakes and poverty repeatedly altered domestic architecture. The result is a severe survival bias. A responsible history therefore cannot begin with the modern paper…

social.title: Mithila Painting and the Twentieth-Century Cultural Economy

social.summary: Mithila painting entered a new historical regime in the twentieth century. The domestic ritual practice discussed in Chapter 47 did not suddenly begin when administrators, craft officials, collectors or museums noticed it. What changed was the social life of the image. A painted wall or floor was tied to a house, ceremony and cycle of renewal; a sheet of paper could be counted, priced, signed, packed, retailed, exhibited, collected and archived. This chapter therefore studies cultural economy rather than origins.…

social.title: Fairs, Markets and Public Culture
